summary: Describes version 2 of the Open Network Computing Remote Procedure Call protocol as deployed, which lets a program call a procedure on another machine as if it were local. It obsoletes RFC 1831 and was on the standards track as a Draft Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ONC RPC lets a client request that a procedure run on a server and receive a reply. RFC 5531 defines the wire messages, authentication fields and record framing, while leaving transport reliability and service discovery to other mechanisms.

subtitle: The message format for calling procedures on another computer with ONC RPC.

tldr.problem: Programs on different computers need agreed messages for naming a procedure, matching its reply and reporting errors or authentication information.
tldr.mechanism: ONC RPC version 2 defines CALL and REPLY messages encoded with XDR. A call identifies a program, version and procedure and carries credentials; a reply carries results or a reason the call failed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5531 records the deployed version 2 protocol without changing its wire format. It obsoletes RFC 1831 and is a Draft Standard updated by RFC 9289.

today: RFC 5531 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1831 and has been updated by RFC 9289. The RFC states that it makes no over-the-wire changes to RPC version 2.

sections.title: What RFC 5531 Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 5531 specifies the message protocol for version 2 of Open Network Computing Remote Procedure Call (ONC RPC). It uses the eXternal Data Representation (XDR) language to describe its messages.

The RFC replaces RFC 1831 as the authoritative description without changing the over-the-wire protocol. It clarifies the RPC language, documents IANA assignment procedures for program and authentication numbers, updates security considerations and describes authentication errors in common use.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC lets one program request a procedure from another computer. This RFC records the message rules for the deployed version 2 protocol.

sections.title: The RPC Model and Transport Limits
sections.content:
A service contains programs; each program provides procedures and may support multiple versions. In a call, the client sends procedure parameters and waits for a reply with results. The protocol does not require this to be synchronous: implementations may process calls asynchronously or use separate server tasks.

RPC specifies message meaning, not how messages travel. It does not provide reliability. With an unreliable transport such as UDP, applications must provide timeouts, retransmission and duplicate detection. A server may compare transaction identifiers to avoid re-executing retransmitted calls, but it can use the identifier only for equality checks.

A reply over TCP indicates the procedure executed exactly once, but receiving no reply does not show whether it executed. Binding a client to a service and choosing transport parameters are outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC defines the request and reply messages, but the transport determines whether they arrive reliably. If a client gets no reply, it cannot know from RPC alone whether the server ran the procedure.

sections.title: CALL and REPLY Messages
sections.content:
Every RPC message starts with a transaction identifier (xid) and a message type: CALL (0) or REPLY (1). A reply repeats the call's xid so the client can match it to the request. The xid is not a sequence number.

A CALL body contains the RPC version, which must equal 2, followed by the program, program version and procedure numbers. It then carries a credential and verifier and the procedure-specific parameters.

A reply is accepted or denied. An accepted reply includes a server verifier and an accept status such as SUCCESS, PROG_UNAVAIL, PROG_MISMATCH, PROC_UNAVAIL, GARBAGE_ARGS or SYSTEM_ERR. A denied reply reports an RPC version mismatch or an authentication error.
sections.plainLanguage: Each call names a program, its version and the procedure to run. The reply repeats the call's identifier and either gives results or explains why the request failed.

sections.title: Authentication Fields and Flavors
sections.content:
A call carries a credential and verifier; a reply carries a response verifier. Each is an opaque_auth value: an authentication-flavor number followed by up to 400 bytes whose meaning is defined by that flavor, not by RPC itself.

AUTH_NONE is required in all implementations and is used when identity is not needed. Implementations may include AUTH_SYS for compatibility. AUTH_SYS can carry a machine name of up to 255 characters, a user ID, a group ID and up to 16 supplementary group IDs.

The RFC warns that AUTH_SYS lacks a verifier that can validate its credential and should not protect services that let clients modify data. Future Standards Track RPC services must require RPCSEC_GSS and an authentication pseudo-flavor with security appropriate to the service.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC leaves the contents of its authentication fields to separate authentication methods. The simple AUTH_SYS method does not prove that its identity information is genuine and is not suitable for protecting services that change data.

sections.title: Program Numbers and IANA
sections.content:
A program number, version number and procedure number identify the requested operation. Program numbers are assigned from ranges for IANA use, local administration, transient use and reserved space. Procedure meanings are defined by each program's own specification.

RFC 5531 transfers authority for program numbers, authentication flavor numbers and authentication status numbers from Sun Microsystems to IANA while preserving prior assignments. IANA begins new program-number assignments at decimal 400000.

Sub-block allocation depends on requested size: up to 100 numbers can be First Come First Served, up to 1000 requires a specification, and larger blocks require IESG approval.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RPC program and authentication method needs a number that does not conflict with another one. IANA maintains the shared number assignments, while local administrators can use a separate range for local programs.

sections.title: Record Marking over TCP
sections.content:
A byte-stream transport such as TCP does not mark the boundary between RPC messages. RPC therefore uses record marking: one RPC message is one record, and a record can contain one or more fragments.

Each fragment starts with a four-byte header. Its highest-order bit indicates whether it is the final fragment, and the remaining 31 bits give the fragment data length in bytes. The data can be split across fragments and assembled into the record by the receiver.

The RFC also describes batching, where a client sends calls without waiting for replies, and broadcast RPC, where a client sends one call and waits for replies from multiple servers.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP sends a continuous byte stream, so RPC adds a header before each fragment to mark its length and whether it ends the record. The receiver uses those markers to separate messages.

sections.title: Describing RPC Programs
sections.content:
The RPC language extends XDR with declarations for programs, versions and procedures. A program contains version definitions; each version contains procedures assigned unsigned constants.

The RFC's example defines a ping program with two versions. One version includes a null procedure and a procedure that asks the server to ping the client and return elapsed time; an earlier version contains only the null procedure.

Procedure and version names and numbers must be unique within their scope. Because current RPC language compilers generally do not support multiple argument types in a procedure declaration, arguments are usually placed in a structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The RPC language lists the programs a server offers, their versions and the numbered procedures in each version. Both client and server can use that description to agree on the requested operation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AUTH_SYS is insecure because its credential cannot be validated with a verifier. AUTH_DH is described as obsolete and insecure. Neither should be recommended for services that allow clients to modify data.

RPCSEC_GSS enables GSS-API mechanisms to secure RPC. RFC 5531 says future non-trivial RPC programs should implement suitable RPCSEC_GSS security, and Standards Track RPC services must require RPCSEC_GSS and a suitable authentication pseudo-flavor.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RPC authentication flavors do not provide enough protection for sensitive operations. The RFC requires Standards Track RPC services to support RPCSEC_GSS with a security level suited to the service.
